newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia stocks end down, but resources shine.
newsitem.headline: Australia stocks end down, but resources shine.

text.p: SPI Futures 2538.0 -8.0 US 30yr 6.91 +0.04
10yrbond futs 92.325 -0.065 Gold NY 343.90 Lon fix 344.75
*Stocks end lower on Dow, but movement mixed as resources shine at expense of sliding banks. Volume 306.92 million, value A$909.58 million, 1054 stocks traded, 324 steady, 283 up, 447 down.
Australian stocks ended lower on Monday with a beaten and bloodied bank sector proving too much for a mining group that showed plenty of polish.
The All Ordinaries index lost 7.1 points or 0.3 percent to 2,531.0, outperforming its Dow counterpart which shed nearly two percent after fears on U.S. interest rate fears spooked traders.
The June SPI futures contract was down eight points at 2,538, a seven point premium to the underlying index.
"The industrials were generally weaker and the miners quite strong," said one senior dealer, summing up a day's action that many said was predictable given the leads available.
"The banks were hit partly because of their results and partly because of the Dow was down - you wouldn't have expected anything else," he said.

With the majors playing a straightforward game, the focus turned to much anticipated debutante, Colonial Ltd CGH.AX, and the bancassurance group failed to disappoint with a spectacular entrance to the Australian market.

Colonial shares listed at A$3.31 and also closed at that price. This compared with an institutional price of A$3.10 and a retail price of A$2.60. Volume was heavy with 32.3 million shares or about 5.6 percent of its issued capital traded.
"There was a lot of trade and some who were there were happy to take profits," said a dealer at one investment bank.

The squeeze on domestic margins confirmed by Westpac Banking Corp and National Australia Bank in their first half results last week saw sellers savage the big four banks yet again, the bank index shedding over two percent.

ANZ Bank was worst hit, dropping 3.8 percent to A$8.017, while Commonwealth Bank lost 36.1 cents to A$13.759. Sector leader National Australia Bank lost 25 cents to A$17.70, while Westpac dropped 13 cents to A$7.11.
Investors were exploring for growth prospects in the miners though and that sector was buoyant, the All Resources index adding 1.2 percent and limiting any broader Dow-inspired losses.
Among the key miners, bellwether and copper major BHP added 34.1 cents to A$19.03, CRA jumped 2.2 percent to A$20.85, while gold/nickel miner WMC added 2.2 percent to A$8.24.
Outside the top rung, major zinc player Pasminco and gold and base metals miner North both added 2.6 percent to A$2.73 and A$4.77 respectively.
In corporate news, food ingredients group Burns Philp was the feature after it announced a restructuring.

Its shares showed some spark, adding six percent to A$1.96 from Friday's eight month low of A$1.85. Traders saying the sale of the spice group and the retirement of its managing director Ian Clack were positive for the group.
"The change of management has to be a positive for the group," said the investment bank dealer.
Falls outnumbered rises by a ratio of about eight to five, while about 31 percent of stocks traded remained steady.
FUTURES/OPTIONS - Futures trade was moderately active as was options trade. Total options traded 36,754 (39,993). Turnover in June SPI contracts totalled 6,220 (6,951).

In other local markets, Australian bond yields succumbed to a typically quiet session ahead of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting where the policy outlook remained clouded. By 5.10 p.m. (0710 GMT), 10 year T-bonds were yielding 7.66 percent, compared to Friday's 7.60 percent.

The Australian dollar was the rather limp filling in a very stale range Monday, sandwiched between exporter and options-related bids and offers from mostly U.S. investment banks and Japanese securities houses. By 5.10 p.m. (0710 GMT), the unit was lying at US$0.7744/49 having barely shifted from an early US$0.7749/54 and Friday's late US$0.7750/55.
